teaser.text: Barclays is a British banking group that earns money by lending, moving money, raising capital and managing investments. The clearest way to understand its business is to follow what customers and markets pay it, what Barclays must pay out, and what remains after risk and capital are counted.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Barclays?

paragraphs.text: The bear case requires credit losses, costs and capital demands to overwhelm the benefit of continued profitability.
The bull case requires recurring income, efficiency and credit quality to improve together.

blocks.heading: What does Barclays earn and give back?

paragraphs.text: Return on tangible equity, or RoTE, measures attributable profit against average tangible equity. Divisional returns sharpen the Group picture: Barclays UK and UK Corporate Bank each earned more than 20% in the first half of 2026, while the Investment Bank earned 15.5% on £29.9bn of allocated tangible equity.
The 2025 dividend was 8.60p per share. Barclays announced £3.7bn of distributions, including £2.5bn of buybacks. After a later £1bn buyback, pro-forma year-end CET1 fell to 14.0%.

paragraphs.text: The current programme combines distributions with other capital choices. Barclays bought a 999-year leasehold interest in One Churchill Place for £750m and announced a £1,000m buyback. It plans to distribute more than £15bn during 2026–2028, including a planned £2bn dividend for 2026. In 2025, subordinated-debt issuance of £1,772m exceeded redemptions of £727m.

The forecast would move toward the bear case if weaker markets or consumer credit raised impairments during 2027–28. Costs remaining above plan, or the cost-to-income ratio failing to reach the low 50s, would reduce RoTE. Higher risk-weighted assets or redress through 2029 would consume capital and constrain buybacks.

blocks.heading: What has Barclays guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management’s current target is approximately £31.5bn of income in 2026. It wants return on tangible equity, or RoTE—the profit earned on shareholders’ equity after goodwill and other intangible assets are removed—to exceed 12% in 2026 and 14% in 2028.

The route combines income growth with efficiency. Barclays targets income growth above 5% a year between 2025 and 2028, a cost-to-income ratio in the low 50s in 2028 and more than £2bn of gross efficiency savings during that period. Its structural hedge spreads deposit-related interest-rate exposure over time; management assumes a 3.5% reinvestment yield and expects the hedge to provide about half of planned income growth.

blocks.heading: Did Barclays keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Barclays reported £700 million of gross cost savings in 2025 against a target of about £500 million. Gross savings come before investment, inflation and other spending, so they do not necessarily equal a fall in total costs. Cross also described higher variable and lower fixed pay for material risk-takers, whose decisions can materially affect the bank’s risk.

blocks.heading: What should Barclays watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: Barclays is scheduled to report Q3 results on 22 October 2026. Investors should watch whether income remains on course, how much structural spending has been recognised and whether consumer businesses are improving alongside the investment bank. Early costs can fit the plan if the promised savings follow; higher costs without them cannot.
